Senses.Explanation: This second position in Dongshan Liangjie's Five Ranks is called “the upright within the biased.” Caoshan Benji defines it as “leaving affairs and entering principle” (偏中正者，舍事入理) and, in his ruler-and-minister scheme, as the minister facing the ruler; both formulas reverse the relation assigned to “the biased within the upright.” Dongshan's rank verse opens with an old woman meeting an ancient mirror at dawn and warns against mistaking the reflected head. Later masters keep the rank active in public questioning rather than leaving it as a diagram: asked “what is the upright within the biased?” (如何是偏中正), Hongzhi Zhengjue answers, “A white-haired old woman is ashamed to look in the mirror” (白髮老婆羞看鏡). Baizhang Ruibai Mingxue also maps the paired ranks onto Linji vocabulary, saying “the upright within the biased removes the object” (偏中正奪境). These are attested definitions, relations, and answers for one named rank; the entry adds no universal teaching beyond them.
Senses.Note: Dongshan Liangjie owns the rank verse; Caoshan Benji owns the direct definition and the ruler-and-minister relation. Those attributions must not be collapsed. Independent lamp collections preserve both, and Caoshan's own recorded sayings preserve his definition. The rank is paired with and reverses “the biased within the upright” in Caoshan's formulas.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Orthodox Line of Chan (禪宗正脉), Caoshan Benji assigns this rank to the minister facing the ruler and contrasts it with the ruler looking at the minister.

Occurrences.Kwic: 正中偏奪人也，偏中正奪境也。
